text.paragraph: Primary care visit for weakness, numbness, and curling of the ring and little fingers of the right hand after a fall onto the elbow, with same-day brain MRI and elbow X-ray. Concerns: He cannot hold the palette or a brush with his right hand and fears he will never paint again; He asks whether this is a stroke. [S]

tr.td: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging: no acute or old infarct, no hemorrhage, and no mass; mild age-appropriate white matter change
Plain X-ray of the right elbow: no fracture or dislocation; a small osteophyte at the medial elbow; normal alignment
Twelve-lead ECG: sinus rhythm at 72 per minute; normal intervals; no atrial fibrillation

Nerve conduction studies of both arms: right ulnar motor conduction velocity 36 m/s across the elbow against 57 m/s in the forearm, with a 38 percent fall in amplitude across the elbow; right ulnar sensory and dorsal ulnar cutaneous responses reduced; median and radial studies and the left ulnar nerve normal

Needle EMG of the right arm: fibrillation potentials and reduced recruitment in the first dorsal interosseous and abductor digiti minimi, milder changes in the flexor digitorum profundus to the little finger, normal flexor carpi ulnaris, and normal abductor pollicis brevis, extensor indicis, and C8 paraspinal muscles
Ultrasound of the right elbow and ulnar nerve: nerve swollen at the medial epicondyle (cross-sectional area 14 mm2 against 7 mm2 in the forearm), no subluxation on flexion, no ganglion, cyst, or mass
Fitting of a night elbow splint (elbow at about 45 degrees of flexion) and a daytime hand-based anti-claw splint for the ring and little fingers
Recombinant zoster vaccine, two-dose series completed

tr.td: Primary care visit for weakness, numbness, and curling of the ring and little fingers of the right hand after a fall onto the elbow, with same-day brain MRI and elbow X-ray
Two-week review with nerve conduction studies, EMG, and nerve ultrasound; diagnosis; hand surgery consultation; start of splinting, hand therapy, and a statin
Four-week review of the ulnar neuropathy on splinting and hand therapy
Nine-week review of the ulnar neuropathy and lipids; shared decision on surgery
Same-day sick visit for red, watery eyes
Same-day assessment for stroke and localization: full neurological examination and NIH Stroke Scale, MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging, X-ray of the right elbow, and an ECG
Hand surgery consultation with nerve conduction studies, EMG, and ultrasound of the ulnar nerve, to confirm the site and severity and to advise on splinting, hand therapy, and surgery

Protect the nerve now: no leaning on the right elbow (a gel elbow pad and a padded armrest at the drawing table), avoid prolonged elbow bending, a towel loosely wrapped around the elbow at night until a splint is made; acetaminophen for pain
Stroke risk-factor screen: blood pressure at every visit with a week of home readings, lipid panel with lipoprotein(a), HbA1c, ECG, and pulse check for atrial fibrillation

Conservative treatment of the ulnar neuropathy for about three months: night elbow splint, daytime anti-claw splint, hand therapy for strength, dexterity, and adapted tools (built-up brush handles, an easel-mounted palette, a lighter brush), with grip and pinch dynamometry and two-point discrimination at each review; no corticosteroid injection
Shared decision on a statin for primary prevention: atorvastatin 20 mg each evening, a lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting, and adherence and muscle-symptom review at each visit

Shared decision on surgery if strength has not improved by about three months: in situ decompression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow (anterior transposition only if the nerve subluxes at operation); tendon transfers to correct the claw only if it persists a year or more after decompression
Falls: a handrail on both sides of the stone staircase, night lighting, footwear review, and a Timed Up and Go at the wellness visit
Stroke excluded and the lesion localized by the second visit
Normal neurological examination apart from the right ulnar territory; MRI brain normal; nerve conduction studies, EMG, and ultrasound confirm ulnar neuropathy at the elbow
Keep working: drawing, writing, and teaching with the left hand, and painting with adapted tools and help
Drawing and teaching fully; painting small panels with an easel palette and built-up brushes
Recovery of ulnar sensation and intrinsic strength, judged at about three months from the injury
Sensation improving; first dorsal interosseous still 3+/5 with clawing at nine weeks; decompression booked
LDL down by 30 to 49 percent on a moderate-intensity statin
LDL 146 to 82 mg/dL (44 percent) after nine weeks of atorvastatin 20 mg
No falls since the injury; handrail fitted and stair lighting added

list.item: Independent in all activities of daily living; cannot hold the palette or a fine brush steadily in the right hand, fumbles buttons and coins, drops objects, and cannot grip a jar lid; drawing and writing with the left hand are unaffected [S]
Alert, articulate, and curious about his own anatomy; fluent speech with normal naming and repetition; worried that he will not paint again; PHQ-2 not done at intake [S]
